name: What Is This Thing? reveal
description: Results-time close-out for the What Is This Thing? patent-drawing set. Names the room's best guess, celebrates the funniest wrong ones, reveals the real invention, inventor, year and patent number from the question's reveal, and tells one or two lines of its story. Bluff-round aware through the bluffRound variable: who held the truth, who fooled the most and who spotted it, with points as scored. Content framing only; the voice comes from the persona (The Comedian on this set).
outputFormat:
Write clean Markdown. The renderer supports bullet lists, numbered lists, **bold**, *italics*, `inline code` and tables, and nothing else here. No HTML, no code fences, no images, no links, no horizontal rules.

Use these cues, because the screen is built for them:

- Write every bullet as a bold lead of two to five words of your own, a colon, then one sentence: for example `**Closest call**: the sentence.` The lead is set as a headline and the rest as its caption on the projector, so a bullet without that shape loses the effect. Never write the words "Lead phrase".
- Keep each bullet to one sentence after the colon. Long bullets wrap badly at projected size.
- Quote the room's own words in *italics* rather than in quotation marks; quotation marks read as scare quotes from the back of a room.
- Never open with a title line, and never add a heading of your own.

Size it before you start: four sections, and none of them runs past two sentences, except What It Really Is on a bluff round, which may take three bullets. If you are running long, cut adjectives before you cut a quoted guess.

outputSections.heading: Best Guess
outputSections.guidance: Open with the guess the room liked best (on a normal round, the top of the ranking), quoted exactly, and one line on why it lands: the logic, the nerve, the sheer invention. Name its author only if a real name is printed beside it. On a bluff round, the best guess is the answer whose author is named after 'Fooled the most' in the bluff round line: say how many voters it fooled, copying the number of votes from that line, and give its author's points from 'Points this round, by author'. Points are not votes; each voter fooled was worth 2 points.

outputSections.heading: Also Worth a Patent
outputSections.guidance: On a bluff round, leave out the truth-holder's answer entirely: that player was handed the real answer, so it is neither a guess nor a close call; it belongs in the next section. Then two or three bullets, each another guess quoted exactly, with one line on why it deserves it. A bullet's bold lead never contains a name; name an author in the sentence only if their guess is in the top three of the ranking or, on a normal round, came close. On a normal round only, a guess that names the same purpose as the reveal came close: say so. On a bluff round, never say any guess came close.

outputSections.heading: What It Really Is
outputSections.guidance: What the invention really is, who patented it, the year and the patent number, exactly as in the reveal. One line. On a bluff round a second line is required, or the reply is malformed: name the truth-holder, say they were handed the real answer and give their points as printed; then, in a new sentence with no figures, say whether their own-words version convinced anyone (the players after 'Spotted the real one' are those it convinced). If they did not answer, say the real answer never made the ballot. The bluff round line again, empty when no bluff ran: {bluffRound}

outputSections.heading: The Story
outputSections.guidance: One or two genuinely interesting lines from the story in the reveal: why it was invented, how it worked or what became of it. Only what the reveal says; a joke about it is fine, a new claim is not. If the reveal has no story beyond the answer itself, write one line on how the best guess compares with the truth, and add no fact.
